as_told: In the 1980s the Pentagon paid $640 for a toilet seat and $435 for a hammer. The two prices became the standard symbols of waste in American military buying.
lesson: The Pentagon pays far more than it should for what it buys.
what_happened: Navy auditors found in 1983 that a contract priced an ordinary claw hammer at $435, and Time reported this in July 1984. Walter Mondale used it in the presidential debate of 21 October 1984 ('$500 for a $5 hammer'). In February 1985 it came out that Lockheed was charging $34,560 for 54 toilet covers for the Navy's P-3C Orion patrol planes, which is $640 each. Time reported that the item was not a toilet seat but a corrosion-resistant plastic case that fits over the whole toilet. Lockheed cut the price to $100 each and gave the Department of Defense a refund of $29,165.

earliest_telling.where: Time, 'Pentagon Markdown' ('Psst—anybody wanna buy a destroyer?'), 23 July 1984
earliest_telling.quote: the payment of $435 for an ordinary claw hammer that Navy auditors discovered last year

original.what: Time's report, written at the time, of the Senate inquiry into the P-3C toilet cover. It describes the item.
original.quote: The item in question was not precisely a toilet seat but a corrosion- resistan t plastic case that fits over a toilet. It is used aboard the Navy’s P-3C Orion antisubmarine planes.

original.what: The same Time report gives Lockheed's total price (54 covers for $34,560, which is $640 each) and the refund.
original.quote: When the contractor learned that Lockheed Corp. was charging $34,560 for 54 toilet covers, he wrote a letter to Roth contending that the units could be purchased at most trailer- home sales outlets for about $25.

original.what: Transcript of the presidential debate in Kansas City, 21 October 1984 (American Presidency Project). Walter Mondale uses the hammer as an example.
original.quote: You pay $500 for a $5 hammer, you're not buying strength.

lesson_verdict.why: The Department of Defense Inspector General found in 2019 that one sole-source supplier, TransDigm, made excess profit on 46 of 47 spare parts it sold to the department, $16.1 million on $26.2 million of sales. The 1985 record also shows overpayment: Lockheed cut the toilet cover price from $640 to $100 and refunded the difference.

source.what: Testimony of the DoD Office of Inspector General at the House Committee on Oversight and Reform hearing 'DOD Inspector General Report on Excess Profits by TransDigm Group, Inc.', 15 May 2019 (GPO hearing record CHRG-116hhrg36511)
source.quote: In total, we determined that for these 46 parts, which cost the DOD $26.2 million, TransDigm earned $16.1 million in excess profit.

search_steps: Web search for the hammer and toilet seat: leads to Time (1984, 1985), James Fairhall's 'The Case for the $435 Hammer' (Washington Monthly, January 1987), Government Executive (1998) and POGO.
Saved Time, 23 July 1984: the $435 claw hammer that Navy auditors found 'last year'. This is the earliest telling I could save.
Saved Time, 18 February 1985: the P-3C toilet cover, Lockheed's $34,560 for 54 covers, the cut to $100 each and the $29,165 refund.
Saved the 21 October 1984 debate transcript from the American Presidency Project: Mondale's '$500 for a $5 hammer'.

Lead only: Fairhall (1987) says the hammer was one line in a 1982 Navy spare-parts contract with Gould Inc.'s Simulation Systems Division for the T-34C flight trainer, and that the $435 came from spreading overhead equally over all items. The full text is behind a paywall (vLex), and I found no contract record, audit or hearing record online, so this explanation is not used as evidence.

One web search for the 1984 Congressional Record and GAO reports on the hammer found no matching record. Two GAO PDFs and the DoD IG PDF returned an HTML error page instead of the report, so I could not read them.
I did not run a separate search for a correction by Time. Lockheed's own reply (13.4 percent profit; price cut to $100) is reported in Time 1985.
Lesson source: GPO record of the 15 May 2019 House Oversight hearing on the DoD Inspector General's TransDigm report. The report itself (DODIG-2019-060) refused automated download.
confidence_note: I could not find a primary record of the hammer contract or of the Navy audit, so the claim that the $435 reflected equal spreading of overhead rests on a later magazine article and is not used here. The 1985 Time article gives the total of $34,560 for 54 covers, not the per-unit $640 directly. The 'toilet seat' was really a molded plastic cover for a whole aircraft toilet. I judged that this detail does not change the lesson, because the price was real and was later cut by more than 80 percent; a reader who takes the lesson to be about ordinary household items would class this as 'changed'.
